questions.question: What is the MVC pattern in Rails?
questions.title: The MVC Pattern
questions.direct_answer: MVC (Model-View-Controller) splits an app into three roles so changes are isolated: Model = data and business rules (Post, with validations, associations, methods); View = presentation (show.html.erb, JSON); Controller = orchestration (routes a request, pulls model data, renders). The flow: a request hits the router, which calls a controller action; the action pulls from models and sets @vars; the action renders a view that reads those @vars. Model changes don't touch presentation; view changes don't touch data rules; controller changes are just wiring. This separation is why large Rails apps stay maintainable — you change one layer without the others breaking.

sections.title: Three Roles, Isolated Changes
sections.content: MVC (Model-View-Controller) splits an app into three roles so changes are isolated: Model is data and business rules (Post, with validations, associations, methods); View is presentation (show.html.erb, JSON); Controller is orchestration (routes a request, pulls model data, renders). The flow: a request hits the router, which calls a controller action; the action pulls from models and sets instance vars; the action renders a view that reads those instance vars. Model changes don't touch presentation; view changes don't touch data rules; controller changes are just wiring. This separation is why large Rails apps stay maintainable — you change one layer without the others breaking.

sections.title: The MVC Flow
sections.content:
request -> router -> controller -> models (@vars) -> view -> response.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  R[request] --> Rt[router]
  Rt --> C[controller: pull models, set @vars]
  C --> M[model: data + rules]
  C --> V[view: presentation]
  V --> Re[response]
```

sections.title: The MVC pattern
sections.content:
```ruby # Model (app/models/post.rb): data + business rules class Post < ApplicationRecord validates :title, presence: true # a rule belongs_to :user # an association def excerpt; body.to_s.truncate(80); end # a method end # Controller (app/controllers/posts_controller.rb): orchestration class PostsController < ApplicationController def show @post = Post.find(params[:id]) # pull from model, set @var # render app/views/posts/show.html.erb (reads @post) end end # View (app/views/posts/show.html.erb): presentation #

<%= @post.title %>

#

<%= @post.excerpt %>

# Flow: request -> router -> controller -> model -> view -> response. # Changes isolate: a model rule change doesn't touch the view; etc. ```

sections.title: Common Mistakes
items: Mixing layers — presentation in the model, queries in the view — defeats the separation.
Putting data fetching in the view (use the controller to set @vars).
Business rules in the controller — they belong in the model or a service.

sections.title: Key Takeaways
items: MVC splits an app: Model (data+rules), View (presentation), Controller (orchestration).
Flow: request -> router -> controller -> models (@vars) -> view -> response.
The controller pulls from models and sets @vars the view reads.
Model changes don't touch presentation; view changes don't touch data rules.
This isolation is why large Rails apps stay maintainable (change one layer).

The flow: a request hits the router, which calls a controller action; the action pulls from models and sets instance vars; the action renders a view that reads those instance vars. A common mistake is mixing layers, like presentation in the model or queries in the view, which defeats the separation.
